The eggs of Chrysoperla carnea are deposited on slender silken stalks, a strategy that reduces cannibalism among emerging larvae. At the point of oviposition, the individual offspring emerges from the egg at an age of 5.1 days [ab = 5.1 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Upon hatching, the neonate larva is remarkably small, measuring just 0.24 centimeters [Lb = 0.24 centimeters] in body length, and possesses a wet weight of only 0.0001 grams [Wwb = only 0.0001 grams]. This minuscule start is typical for neuropteran larvae, which must immediately begin hunting aphids and other soft-bodied prey to fuel their rapid growth. The first-instar larva, weighing barely a tenth of a milligram, begins active foraging within hours of eclosion. The initial body mass represents a critical life-history bottleneck, as mortality during the first few days is substantial, often exceeding 50 percent in field populations due to starvation or predation. Nevertheless, survivors embark on an aggressive feeding regimen, quickly increasing in body size as they consume prey items that often rival their own body dimensions. The low initial mass of only 0.0001 grams [Wwb = only 0.0001 grams] underscores the vulnerability of this life stage and the importance of abundant aphid prey at the time of egg hatch for successful recruitment.

Under the controlled thermal conditions of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the larvae of the common green lacewing progress through three instars before reaching the prepupal stage. A period of 11 days  elapses from hatch to pupation, during which intense feeding fuels rapid dimensional growth, culminating in a final larval body length of 0.71 centimeters  at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. The wet weight of the pupa itself has been measured at 0.0083 grams , though considerable variation exists, with some pupae weighing as little as 0.00708 grams  and others reaching 0.00946 grams  depending on nutritional history during the larval stage. A further observation places pupal wet weight at 0.0084 grams , consistent with the central tendency. Following metamorphosis within the silken cocoon, the interval from pupation to adult emergence at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] spans 11.5 days , culminating in eclosion of the imago.

The imago of Chrysoperla carnea emerges with a body length of 0.724 centimeters  and a dry weight of 0.003107 grams , the latter reflecting water loss upon desiccation and serving as a proxy for structural biomass. The wet weight at emergence has been reported at 0.0116 grams ; a second measurement records it at 0.00896 grams , indicating variability in resource acquisition during the larval stage. The time elapsed since hatching to adult emergence is 17.9 days  at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], representing total larval and pupal development. Once emerged, the adult enters a pre-reproductive phase, with first egg release occurring 4.2 days after eclosion  at the same temperature at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This delay allows completion of cuticular sclerotization and reproductive system maturation. If growth were to continue unimpeded beyond emergence, the hypothetical asymptotic wet weight for this species would be estimated at 0.08 grams , a value that vastly exceeds the actual emergential mass and underscores the cessation of somatic growth at metamorphosis typical of holometabolous insects.

At a rearing temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the developmental timeline accelerates. The time from hatch to pupation is 8 days , and in some trials just 7 days , a striking acceleration attributed to elevated metabolic rates at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The interval from pupation to adult emergence at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] lasts 9 days , shorter than the 11.5-day period at 23 °C. These temperature-dependent responses highlight the plasticity of lacewing ontogeny, permitting rapid generation turnover in warm seasons. The ultimate wet weight achieved by mature adults is approximately 0.0297 grams [Wwi = approximately 0.0297 grams], while a closely comparable record gives 0.0296 grams [Wwi = 0.0296 grams], suggesting a consistent mass ceiling. Under high-temperature conditions typical of summer field populations (32 °C [T = 32 °C]), females produce approximately 247.44 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 247.44 eggs per day], a remarkably high daily output for a neuropteran, underpinning rapid population growth during aphid outbreaks.

Reproductive rates in Chrysoperla carnea exhibit strong temperature dependence. At 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females oviposit approximately 27.7 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 27.7 eggs per day], derived from a clutch of 1264 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 1264 eggs] , one clutch every 45.6 days [F_R_i = one clutch every 45.6 days], though more commonly expressed as a daily rate. Another estimate places the daily production at approximately 14.4 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 14.4 eggs per day] from a clutch of 694.4 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 694.4 eggs] every 48.3 days. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], daily oviposition reaches a mean of 15.67 eggs per day [Ri = 15.67 eggs per day], though another estimate records 8.67 eggs per day [Ri = 8.67 eggs per day], possibly reflecting differences in adult nutrition or experimental conditions. The adult lifespan following emergence at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] has been documented at 51.7 days , while other records indicate a mean of 48.3 days , suggesting a typical adult longevity of approximately seven weeks under optimal conditions before senescence and natural death of the imago occur.
